conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-tested questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)**. It’s simply ten gentle questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. Anything you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, and you can pause anytime. Ready for the first one?

1. Over the last week, have you still been able to enjoy things you usually like—music, a favorite show, a walk outside—or has that pleasure slipped away?

Hi Sarah. I… I still enjoy some things, just not as much as I used to. Like, I’ll put on the playlist I loved during pregnancy and it feels kind of flat—almost like I’m listening through a wall. Same with the little walks I used to take around the block; they help a bit, but I don’t get that lift I used to. I can still laugh if I really try, but it takes effort.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I’ve laughed a few times—like when my partner made that silly joke about the diapers yesterday—but it doesn’t come as easily. Mostly I have to force a chuckle, and then I feel kind of guilty for even pretending to enjoy myself when I’m so tired.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I tell myself I should be excited about little outings—like the moms’ group on Thursday—but when I think about actually going, it just feels like another chore. I don’t have that “can’t-wait” feeling I used to get, even for small stuff like having coffee with a friend.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah… like yesterday when she wouldn’t settle for her nap, I kept thinking, “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not reading her cues right.” I know babies are fussy, but I still caught myself wondering if a “better mom” would’ve figured it out faster.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I’ve had that a few times this week—like when she sneezed a couple times in a row and my mind jumped straight to “What if she’s getting really sick?” or I’ll lie down at night and suddenly worry her breathing sounds different, even though she’s fine. It’s not constant, but it pops up out of nowhere and my heart starts racing.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of nights this week I’ve woken up suddenly with that tight-chest, can’t-catch-my-breath feeling—like I’m on the edge of something bad happening—even though nothing’s wrong. It passes after a minute or two, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… some afternoons, after a night of only broken sleep, everything feels like too much. I’ll be trying to fold laundry while she’s fussing, and suddenly the pile looks enormous and my heart starts racing. I haven’t fallen apart, but I do catch myself thinking, “I can’t keep up,” even with the little stuff.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s more that I’m so tired I should drop off, but my mind keeps circling—did I sterilize the bottles, is she breathing, will she wake up the second I close my eyes? I end up lying there for an hour or two, and when I finally do sleep it’s really light, so I wake up groggy and on edge.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way some days—like this heavy, teary cloud settles in. It’s not every moment, but I’ll be feeding her and suddenly feel weepy, or I’ll see other moms posting happy pictures and think, “Why don’t I feel that upbeat?” The sadness comes and goes, maybe every other day or so.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not a lot—just twice this week. Once was when she wouldn’t nap and I felt completely stuck on the couch; the tears slipped out before I could stop them. The other time was after my mom left and the house felt so quiet and overwhelming. It’s not every day, but when it hits, it feels like a sudden release of all the tension.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’m exhausted and overwhelmed sometimes, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again and be able to enjoy my baby.

You've shared that the joy you once felt has dulled: laughter feels forced, outings seem like chores, and a <sym>heavy, teary cloud</sym> drifts in every other day. You blame yourself when your baby fusses, wake with racing thoughts about her health, and lie awake for hours even though you're exhausted. Although you love your daughter and are free of self-harm thoughts, the sadness, worry, and sense of being overwhelmed are clearly wearing you down.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional, forced laughter with guilt, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment, describing even pleasant events as feeling like chores and lacking any "can't-wait" feeling, aligning with "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurrent self-blame "sometimes" for normal infant behavior, mapping to "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes specific, recurring instances of sudden, unbidden worries about baby's health that trigger physical anxiety; fits "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden nighttime panic with physical symptoms, happening a few times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent episodes of feeling overwhelmed and unable to keep up, but still managing without total collapse, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly inability to fall and stay asleep directly linked to persistent anxious/unhappy thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring sadness every other day, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 19/30 places you well above the ≥14 cutoff that signals probable major depressive or anxiety disorder in the postpartum period. You endorse core symptoms of <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), prominent guilt, sleep disruption not solely due to infant care, low mood, and recurrent crying, plus comorbid anxiety with sudden panic. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to review these results
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for evaluation and possible therapy or medication
3. Begin brief daily mood/activity log to bring to your visit
4. Practice 10-minute wind-down routine (dim lights, no screens, slow breathing) to ease <sym>initial insomnia</sym>
5. Share these EPDS findings with a trusted support person so they can help coordinate care
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, approximately 1–2 weeks after delivery  
Date: [today’s date]  
Instrument: EPDS-10 (self-report plus clinician follow-up)

Symptoms endorsed
- Anhedonia / low enjoyment: reports minimal spontaneous laughter; anticipates outings as chores  
- Persistent low mood: “heavy, teary cloud” every other day; spontaneous crying twice this week  
- Guilt / self-blame: attributes infant fussiness to personal inadequacy (“better mom” narrative)  
- Excessive anxiety: sudden health worries about infant, racing heart; repeated nocturnal panic episodes  
- Feeling overwhelmed: routine tasks “too much,” heart racing while folding laundry  
- Sleep disruption: initial insomnia linked to intrusive worries, light/unrefreshing sleep  
- No suicidal or self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)

Pattern
Consistent with mixed depressive and anxious symptomatology of moderate intensity; functional impact on sleep, self-care, and emotional bonding.

Risk flags
- Daily sadness and anhedonia  
- Anxiety with panic equivalents  
- Sleep loss driven by rumination  
- Absence of self-harm thoughts (protective)

Screening impression
Elevated scores on EPDS items for depression and anxiety; clinical cutoff likely exceeded. Recommends immediate formal assessment (PHQ-9/GAD-7) and referral to perinatal mental-health specialty for evaluation of probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety. No safety concerns at present.
